title: Baker Street
year_note: City to City came out on 20 January 1978 and the single on 3 February.

notes.made: Recorded in 1977 at Chipping Norton Studios in Oxfordshire, produced by Rafferty and Hugh Murphy. Raphael Ravenscroft played the eight-bar alto riff (Pete Zorn, the first choice, wasn't available) and was reportedly paid £27. Ravenscroft later said most of it was an old blues riff; Rafferty said it was his line and he sang it to him. Hugh Burns played the guitar solo and Henry Spinetti the drums.
notes.context: Rafferty wrote it while trying to get out of his Stealers Wheel contracts, and he often stayed at a friend's flat on Baker Street in Marylebone. City to City was his first release of any kind since 1975. 'Baker Street' reached 3 in the UK and 2 in the US, stuck behind Andy Gibb's 'Shadow Dancing', and on 8 July 1978 the album knocked Saturday Night Fever off No. 1. It won the 1979 Ivor Novello for best song musically and lyrically.

listen_for.note: Ravenscroft's alto riff, the £27 part everyone remembers and that brought the sax back into TV ads.
Hugh Burns; Slash has said it fed into his 'Sweet Child o' Mine' solo.
It runs 6:06, nearly two minutes longer than the single, with more room for the sax and guitar.

leads_to.title: Stuck in the Middle with You
leads_to.why: Rafferty's earlier band, the one whose contracts he was escaping when he wrote Baker Street.

notes.unverified: Panel line says Rafferty 'comes from Glasgow'; he was born in Paisley, near Glasgow, and the record was made in Oxfordshire. The Slash and TV-ads claims are from the Wikipedia article's legacy section.

culture.title: No. 2, behind Shadow Dancing
culture.line: It reached 2 on the Hot 100, held off by Andy Gibb's 'Shadow Dancing', and 3 in the UK. It was No. 1 in Canada for four weeks.

culture.title: Ivor Novello
culture.line: It won the 1979 Ivor Novello Award for best song musically and lyrically.

culture.title: Undercover
culture.line: Undercover's 1992 dance version, produced by Steve Mac, reached 2 in the UK.

culture.title: Foo Fighters
culture.line: Foo Fighters covered it in 1998 for the 'My Hero' single, with the sax part played on electric guitar.
